title: Good Ayis Are Always on the Job — Domestic-Service Consultants Don't Sell Information
dek: Domestic work is a supply-led industry: good ayis never reach the open market, and the consultant's real challenge isn't closing the deal but handling replacements after the sale; employers and ayis alike are just passers-through of wages.
why: A frontline post-00s domestic-service consultant lays out a neglected essential industry: matching mechanics, pricing, off-platform deals, boundaries — high information density, and the second half is worth more.
who: Dual-income families hiring or about to hire a yuesao or yuer sao; founders and investors watching domestic services and local life services.
skip: From 1:35:37, the part about twins-family interviews over picture books is more anecdote than analysis — fast-forward.

points.h: Good ayis are always on the job
points.body: This market has a circulation paradox: ayis with good reviews never reach the open market. She works for one family for two or three years, and the moment she leaves she's referred straight to the next one. Those actually circulating on the market are often the ones nobody is satisfied with after looking around. So the industry's core contradiction is supply — where good ayis come from and how they get discovered. A domestic-service company is essentially a human resources company: it has to recruit, train and re-match.

points.h: Every woman in this trade has a story
points.body: The ayi profile clusters in third- and fourth-tier cities and even poor villages, aged 30 to 45, many divorced or single. Live-in sisters spend little time with their own families, giving their time to another family instead. Two obvious traits mark their choice of this work: they like children, and they hunger to earn — not a comfortable life back home farming and drinking tea, but packing everything they own, buying a green-skin train ticket and squeezing into Shanghai.

There has to be a sense of boundaries and proportion between ayi and employer — not just for the ayi, but for the employer too. Some people spoil the ayi past the line, but everyone takes a mile when given an inch. More subtly, a live-in ayi is together with the family 24 hours a day and may know more about the household's private life than relatives do — that's a lot of pressure. Some mothers are doing widow-style parenting with the dad absent, and it's the ayi who keeps the mother company longer; the two become teammates.

points.h: Employer and ayi are both passers-through of wages
points.body: To the employer it feels like being a passers-through of wages, and it's the same for the ayi: the monthly WeChat transfer comes in and immediately goes out — two children's tuition first, then the household living expenses. For many yuesao and yuer sao, the income is the family's most important or even only source, which is why her role as wife within the family structure is so dominant. That also explains why employers care about the ayi's family background — you're not hiring a company employee, and her stability is directly tied to her family situation.

points.h: How a ten-page job spec doesn't scare the ayi away
points.body: The longest yuesao job spec I've seen ran a full ten pages, yet the price was only the market average. Employers think that if they write out every minute and second, the ayi will execute like a robot — but people are emotional. The consultant won't forward it directly; she'll first send a voice message to lay the groundwork: asking about luggage, giving directions, telling her the client says just arrive at this time, then explaining that company rules require the employer to list requirements and she can come to me anytime with questions. That way the ayi feels she's been handed a guidebook, not interrogated.

points.h: Closing the deal is easy; replacing someone is the test
points.body: Yuesao bookings are advance orders; yuer sao jobs are mostly urgent — an ayi only enters the market after leaving her previous family, so demand is pressing. Many employers assume that whoever is urgently available must be inferior, when in fact it's often the booked one who's the fake. Closing a deal isn't hard for a consultant: as long as the employer has a need and a budget, someone can always be found. The real difficulty is long-term after-sales — you can be thrilled in the interview and still, with some probability, be let down later, and handling replacements is what truly tests a consultant's level.

points.h: The hardest deal requires reading the family's core relationship
points.body: The hardest deal I've had: a single-mother female executive who wanted a daytime child development companion, but also expected this person to do housework to cleaning-standard results — while the companion's hourly rate is twice a cleaner's. The consultant dealt with an assistant, and the core need was also shaped by the executive's mother. The compromise was cleaners for cleaning and companions for companionship, but the mother still had to be won over. The person finally found was the polar opposite of the original spec — originally under 35 with a bilingual kindergarten teaching background; in the end, a sister close to 50 with an education background and live-in experience.

points.h: Yuesao start at 15,000; yuer sao depends on age
points.body: In first-tier cities a yuesao's 26-day contract price is generally 15,000–16,000 or more; for one with two or three years' experience who has genuinely cared for newborns, it's basically 15,000 to 20,000. Shanghai rates for yuer sao: beginners from 7,000, experienced hands depending on age, skills and work history, basically 8,000-plus; stack on English, bilingual, early education or driving requirements and it's 10,000-plus. Prices have risen in recent years partly because more highly educated people are entering the trade, and partly because supply still falls short of demand.

points.h: Consensus and trade norms are what this industry lacks most
points.body: The live-in norm is that the ayi brings her own personal items and the employer provides big items like bedding, but the two sides haven't formed a consensus yet. Some think it's lovely when an ayi who's been there a long time grows attached and spends her own wages buying things for the baby; others find it too close. A common situation is a mother who's unhappy that the child is too attached to the ayi. Consultant training teaches this: the person in a family who should have the closest contact is the mother — not the father, not the grandparents.

points.h: Young people doing domestic work is long past being a meme
points.body: By the time something becomes a meme, the number of people doing it is already beyond what you'd imagine. The contraction of the tutoring industry fed a lot of talent into domestic services; child development companions are very young, a cohort in their twenties, because jobs are hard to find and this trade provides room and board and you're responsible for just one child. After five to eight years of live-in experience, yuying shi and yuesao get older and can't keep up with the kids, so they shift toward trainer roles. But whether you do yuying shi or child development companion, it's very hard to build a three-to-five-year career plan.

quotes.text: For the employer it's like being a passers-through of wages, and for many ayis it's really the same.
Because an ayi is a person — people aren't machines, people are in a state where they have emotions.
Closing a deal isn't hard for us — we can always help an employer find someone they're satisfied with, as long as they have a need, right, and a budget. But the hard part usually comes later.
I think right now neither side of the employment relationship has really formed this consensus, hasn't yet accumulated to the point of knowing roughly what state this industry is in.
